explanations.answer: The faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul says he is an apostle “…for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness…” (Titus 1:1). That's the purpose he names right in his opening line. I wish my old resume had been that tidy.

explanations.answer: The growth of the churches and their care for the poor
explanations.explanation: Those sound like fine things, friend, but they aren't what Paul says here. He says his work is “…for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness…” (Titus 1:1). He puts faith and knowing the truth right up front.

explanations.answer: The law of Moses and its customs of old
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't mention that in his opening, baker. He calls himself a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ. Then he says his work is “…for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness…” (Titus 1:1).

Right on the money, friend. Paul says the promise of eternal life came from “…God, who cannot lie…” (Titus 1:2). The One who made the promise is the One who cannot lie. A promise from someone like that is one you can count on.

Paul doesn't say that here, baker. In this verse he says the promise of eternal life came from “…God, who cannot lie…” (Titus 1:2). Ruling the nations isn't in the verse. The line is about the God who promised, and that He cannot lie.

Paul doesn't say that in this verse, friend. What he says is that God “cannot lie,” and that this God promised eternal life (Titus 1:2). He puts the spotlight on the promise and on the One who made it.

True, baker. Paul says God promised eternal life “…before time began.” (Titus 1:2). That's older than any recipe I've ever baked, and older than the oven too. Before the clock even started, the promise was already made.

This one is true, friend. Paul says God “…promised before time began.” (Titus 1:2). So the promise of eternal life was made before the clock even started ticking. Don't sweat it, I once misread an oven dial for a whole week.
Yes, baker. Paul says the proclamation was entrusted to him “…by the command of God our Savior.” (Titus 1:3). The command came from God. That's the source Paul names.
Paul doesn't name them, friend. He says the preaching was entrusted to him “…by the command of God our Savior.” (Titus 1:3). The command came straight from God.
Peter isn't the answer, baker. Paul says the preaching was entrusted to him “…by the command of God our Savior.” (Titus 1:3). That's who gave the order. Peter isn't named in this verse.
That's the one, baker. Paul says Titus was to “…appoint elders in every town…” (Titus 1:5). Every town, no skipping. That's a lot of towns and a lot of appointing.

Judges is a fair guess for a leader, friend, but Paul uses a different word. He tells Titus to “…appoint elders in every town…” (Titus 1:5). Titus was left in Crete to set in order what was unfinished, and appointing elders is part of that.
Not priests, baker. Paul says Titus was left in Crete to “…appoint elders in every town…” (Titus 1:5). Elders is the word on the page. Titus was also there to set in order what was unfinished.

It's actually false, friend. Paul says an elder must be “…the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). Home life is right there in the requirements. It isn't a side note, so no hiding the mess behind a nice church smile.
False is right, baker. Paul says an elder must be blameless, “…the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). His home gets named in the requirements. It counts.

Yes, baker. Paul says the elder has “…children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). Then he adds that they must not be open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. His household gets looked at, not just him.

explanations.answer: They should be grown and married
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say a word about that, friend. He says the elder has “…children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). Their ages and whether they're married never come up.

explanations.answer: They should be trained to teach
explanations.explanation: That's not in the verse, baker. What Paul says is that an elder has “…children who are believers…” (Titus 1:6). Teaching comes up later, but it's about the elder himself.

That one's false, friend. Paul says an overseer must be “not quick-tempered” (Titus 1:7). It's right there on the list, with no loopholes. I once argued with an oven timer, so I'm not throwing stones.
False it is, baker. Paul says an overseer must be above reproach, and “not quick-tempered” is on the list of what he must not be (Titus 1:7). Being above reproach in other ways doesn't cancel it out.

True, baker. Paul says, “Instead, he must be hospitable…” (Titus 1:8). After a long list of what not to be, he turns to what an overseer must be. Hospitable means making room for people, and my bakery is always open for that.

It's true, friend. Right after the NOT list, Paul says, “Instead, he must be hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined.” (Titus 1:8). Hospitable is on the MUST list, the first thing named.

explanations.answer: To encourage others and refute those who contradict it
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says the overseer holds firmly to the faithful word “…so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.” (Titus 1:9). The word is for building people up and for answering those who push against it.

explanations.answer: To win every debate and gain followers in town
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, friend. He says the overseer holds to the faithful word “…so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.” (Titus 1:9). The goal is encouraging others, not collecting a fan club.

explanations.answer: To keep the teaching hidden away from outsiders
explanations.explanation: Hiding it isn't what Paul says, baker. He says the overseer holds firmly to the word “…so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.” (Titus 1:9). Encouraging others and refuting those who contradict are the reasons the verse gives. Keeping the teaching hidden isn't one of them.

Right, friend. Paul says of those full of empty talk and deception that they “…must be silenced.” (Titus 1:11). He goes on to say that for the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not. That's the situation Titus is facing.
Paul doesn't say welcomed, baker. Of those full of empty talk and deception, he says they “…must be silenced.” (Titus 1:11). Silenced is the word he uses for them. Welcoming isn't in the verse.
No excuses in this verse, friend. Paul says these men “…must be silenced.” (Titus 1:11). He doesn't tell Titus to let it slide.

You got it, baker. Paul says, “For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households…” (Titus 1:11). So they're after something for themselves, and whole households pay for it. That's a steep price for someone else's profit.

Paul never says that, friend. He says it's “For the sake of dishonorable gain…” that they undermine entire households (Titus 1:11). The verse points to gain for themselves, not to a grudge against Paul. Whole households get undermined so somebody else can profit.
That's not in the verse, baker. Paul says they “…undermine entire households…” and do it “For the sake of dishonorable gain…” (Titus 1:11). No word about wanting a seat as an elder.
True, baker. After quoting the prophet, Paul says, “This testimony is true.” (Titus 1:13). He's leaning on the quote to make his point. And then he gives Titus what to do about it.
It's true, friend. Right after the quote, Paul says, “This testimony is true.” (Titus 1:13). He doesn't brush it off. He says it's true and moves straight to what Titus should do.
That's the one, baker. Paul says, “Therefore rebuke them sternly…” (Titus 1:13). Sternly is the word he chooses. He adds the reason too, which is that they will be sound in the faith.

Paul doesn't say that, friend. He tells Titus, “Therefore rebuke them sternly…” (Titus 1:13). The instruction is to rebuke them, not to send them away. The verse says the aim is that they will be sound in the faith.
Paul doesn't say to leave them alone, baker. He says, “Therefore rebuke them sternly…” (Titus 1:13). What he tells Titus to do is rebuke them. The verse says nothing about leaving them be.

explanations.answer: So they will be sound in the faith
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul says to rebuke them sternly “…so that they will be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:13). The aim is for them to be sound in the faith. It's a hard word with a hopeful goal behind it.

explanations.answer: So the whole town sees them shamed
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, baker. He says to rebuke them sternly “…so that they will be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:13). Being sound in the faith is the stated goal.

explanations.answer: So they will leave the church for good
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says, friend. He says the stern rebuke is “…so that they will be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:13). The goal he names is that they become sound in the faith. Leaving the church isn't in the verse.
Yes, baker. Paul wants them to “…pay no attention to Jewish myths…” (Titus 1:14). Not a little attention, none. That's the word for the first blank.
That's the word, friend. Paul says not to pay attention to “…the commands of men who have rejected the truth.” (Titus 1:14). Those commands come from men who turned the truth down.
Paul doesn't say feasts, baker. The verse says “Jewish myths,” and that's the word that fits the first blank (Titus 1:14). Feasts aren't mentioned.

Not prophets, friend. Paul says “Jewish myths” for the first blank, and the second blank is “truth” (Titus 1:14). A prophet does come up earlier in the passage, when Paul quotes one of their own prophets (Titus 1:12), but not in this verse.
Elders are in the passage, baker, but not in this verse. Paul says “Jewish myths” and “…men who have rejected the truth.” (Titus 1:14). Elders were Titus's job back in verse 5.

That's it, baker. Paul says, “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.” (Titus 1:15). Two very different outcomes in one sentence, and 'nothing' is the strong one.
Close, friend, but that's the pure side of the sentence. Paul says, “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.” (Titus 1:15). The second half flips it.
Paul goes further than that, baker. He says, “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure.” (Titus 1:15). Not even a little something, just nothing.
That's false, friend. Paul says, “Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled.” (Titus 1:15). Both of them, the mind and the conscience. Neither one gets a pass.
False is right, baker. Paul says, “…both their minds and their consciences are defiled.” (Titus 1:15). So the minds aren't clean either. The word 'both' covers the two of them.
You got it, baker. Paul says, “They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.” (Titus 1:16). Words can say one thing while a life says another. The actions give them away.
Paul doesn't say that, friend. He says, “They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.” (Titus 1:16). What gives them away is their actions.
That's not in the verse, baker. Paul says, “They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.” (Titus 1:16). It's their actions, not anything they say about the apostles.
It's false, friend. Paul says these men are “…detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.” (Titus 1:16). Any good deed, so that's a strong word. That's the last line of the whole chapter.

False, baker. Paul says they are “…detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.” (Titus 1:16). He doesn't leave a few good deeds on the table for them. The verse also says they profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him.
